chunks: What are linear motors?. The question: What are linear motors?
A linear motor makes force in a straight line instead of torque (a turning force) on a shaft. It is like a normal motor that has been cut open and rolled out flat.
A stationary track holds magnets, and a sliding part carries coils. Switching the coils in order pushes the slider along the track with no gears or screws in between.
Imagine slicing a cardboard tube lengthwise and unrolling it into a flat sheet. The curved wall of the tube becomes a straight strip.
A linear motor does the same to a rotary motor: the round stationary part becomes a straight track, and the spinning part becomes a slider.
The analogy has one catch: the flattened version needs a position sensor along the track, since there is no shaft to put a rotation sensor on.
A flat PM linear motor.
Three coil groups (A, B, C) on the forcer are energised in sequence by position-dependent currents, creating a travelling magnetic wave that pulls the forcer along the alternating-pole magnet track.
The encoder gives the position needed for commutation and closed-loop control.
Forcer (slider): the moving part that carries the coils. Track: the stationary strip of alternating magnets.
Lorentz force: the push on a wire carrying current through a magnetic field: F equals BIL , field strength B (in teslas, T) times current I times wire length L .
Direct drive: no gearbox, belt or screw between motor and load. Linear encoder: a sensor that reports position along the track.
Suppose a wire 0. 2 m long sits in a 0. 5 T field and carries 10 amps. The force is F equals BIL = 0. 5 times 10 times 0. 2 = 1 N .
Double the current to 20 amps and the force doubles to 2 N.
That straight-line push is what moves the slider, and the force is proportional to current just like torque in a rotary motor.
That is the whole idea: force from current in a magnetic field, laid out in a line.
"A linear motor is a rotary motor unrolled flat: a magnet track and a coil carrier, the forcer, that moves along it.
Force is proportional to current, F equals K fI , and the moving coil generates a back-EMF K ev , same as a rotary motor.
The big win is direct drive: no lead screw, belt or gearbox, so no backlash and very high speed and precision.
The downsides are cost, heat, limited force without gearing, strong magnet attraction and needing a linear encoder. Think wafer stages, voice coils and maglev."
